title: Knight against pawn
summary: Where the knight stops the pawn, why the edge is its enemy, how the king helps, and when the knight still mates.
part.front.title: In front of the pawn
part.front.summary: A knight on the queening square, or watching it, stops even a pawn on the seventh.
part.side.title: From the side, with a fork
part.side.summary: When the front is taken, the knight watches the square from the side and sets up a fork. From behind it fails.
part.knightPawn.title: The knight's pawn
part.knightPawn.summary: Near the edge the knight has fewer squares: either it reaches the right one, or the pawn gets through.
part.rookPawn.title: The rook's pawn
part.rookPawn.summary: The knight's worst enemy: on the sixth it can still be held; on the seventh, with the king beside it, almost never.
part.king.title: The king helps
part.king.summary: The knight gains time, the king arrives, and even losing the knight draws with the black king locked in the corner.
part.mate.title: When the knight wins
part.mate.summary: Stamma's mate: the king trapped in the corner, in front of its own rook's pawn.
part.recap.title: Summary and a game
part.recap.summary: Three rules for your games and one ending to hold in the practical challenge.
step.t_front: White to move. The black pawn is on the seventh, one step from queening, and the white king is far away. Can the knight hold alone? Where does it need to be?
step.t_front.hint1: The pawn queens on d1. Which squares can the knight on b2 reach in one move?
step.t_front.hint2: The safest square for stopping a pawn is the square where it wants to queen.
step.frontWhy: 1.Nd1. The knight sits on the queening square and the pawn is frozen. The black king can attack the knight, but it does not have to stay there: from f2, e3, b2 or c3 it still watches d1, and it often comes back with check. Against a centre or bishop's pawn the knight has squares on both sides for this.
step.d_front: Watch the knight hold the pawn with no help at all, while the white king takes a walk.
step.d_front.m1: 1.Nd1. In front of the pawn, on the queening square.
step.d_front.m2: The black king attacks the knight.
step.d_front.m3: 2.Nf2. The knight steps away, but from f2 it still watches d1.
step.d_front.m4: 2...Kc3. Black tries to come closer from the other side.
step.d_front.m5: 3.Kb6. My king is on its way, but there is no hurry: the knight can cope alone.
step.d_front.m6: 3...Kd4. The black king goes after the knight.
step.d_front.m9: 5.Nd1, check. The knight returns to the queening square and gains the tempo.
step.d_front.m11: 6.Nb2. From b2 the knight also watches d1, now from the other side of the pawn.
step.d_front.m13: 7.Nc4, check, and the knight attacks the pawn.
step.d_front.m14: The king steps out of check, and the pawn is left undefended.
step.d_front.m15: 8.Nxd2. King and knight against king: a draw.
step.frontMove: White to move and draw. The pawn is on the seventh. Bring the knight to where it watches the queening square, then onto it.
step.frontMove.hint: The pawn queens on d1. Look for the square from which the knight sees d1 without being taken by the king.
step.frontMove.done: That's it. From c3 the knight was watching d1, and now it sits on it. The pawn cannot move.
step.t_side: White to move. The black king is on c1, in front of its own pawn: the knight cannot sit on the queening square. Is there still a draw?
step.t_side.hint1: If the pawn queens, the knight may still have a fork: a check that hits the king and the new queen at once.
step.t_side.hint2: First a check to get the king off c1. Then find the square from which the knight watches c2 and b3.
step.sideWhy: 1.Ne2+ drives the king off c1, and 2.Nd4 puts the knight to the side. From d4 it watches c2 and b3. If the pawn queens on c1, 3.Nb3+ checks the king on d2 and attacks the queen: a fork. If the king steps aside, the knight takes the pawn. I call this side control: the knight is not in front, but queening costs the queen.
step.d_side: Watch side control work to the end.
step.d_side.m1: 1.Ne2, check. The black king must leave the front of the pawn.
step.d_side.m2: 1...Kd2, defending the pawn and attacking the knight.
step.d_side.m3: 2.Nd4. From the side: it watches c2 and b3.
step.d_side.m5: 3.Nb3, check, and the queen on c1 is attacked. A fork.
step.d_side.m6: The king steps out of check.
step.d_side.m7: 4.Nxc1. The new queen lived for one move. Draw.
step.sideBehind: What if the knight watches from behind? 1.Nd3+ followed by 2.Nc5 looks similar, but it is not: from behind there is no fork on the queening square, the black king walks up to the knight, and it loses touch with the pawn. That is why, in this position, only 1.Ne2+ draws. In front is best; from the side still works; from behind it is almost always too late.
step.sideMove: White to move and draw. The black king protects the pawn on c2. Use the check and the fork.
step.sideMove.hint: Start with a check that puts the knight in sight of b3 and c2.
step.sideMove.done: Very good. With the check and the fork set up, the knight never lost sight of the queening square, and the pawn does not get through.
step.t_averbakh: White to move. Now the pawn is a knight's pawn, and the white king is far away. Does the knight on f5 get there in time? By which route?
step.t_averbakh.hint1: Near the edge the knight has fewer squares. Think about where it can watch b1 without being chased away.
step.t_averbakh.hint2: From the a-file the knight sees b1. Count the moves to get there.
step.averbakhWhy: This position is Averbakh's. Only 1.Nd6 draws: the knight goes to b5 and a3, and from a3 it watches b1. When the black king attacks, the knight jumps to b1, in front of the pawn, and back to a3 with check. The route matters: any other move arrives one tempo late.
step.d_averbakh: Watch the knight arrive in time, with just one move to spare.
step.d_averbakh.m3: 2.Nb5. Now a3 is one jump away.
step.d_averbakh.m5: 3.Na3. From a3 the knight watches b1.
step.d_averbakh.m6: 3...Kc3. The king wants to chase the knight away.
step.d_averbakh.m7: 4.Nb1, check. The knight sits on the queening square.
step.d_averbakh.m9: 5.Na3, check again, and b1 is still covered.
step.d_averbakh.m11: 6.Nb1. Black cannot get out of this: a draw.
step.knightPawnLoss: Now the opposite: here Black is to move and wins with 1...b2. After 2.Nd2+ Kc1 the black king attacks the knight and guards b1; the knight has no fork and no safe square from which to watch b1, and the pawn queens. With a knight's pawn, reaching the right square is a matter of one tempo.
step.kpMove: White to move and draw. The g-pawn is on the seventh. Bring the knight to the square that watches g1, then onto g1.
step.kpMove.hint: The queening square is g1. On the edge side, only one square watches it without the black king taking it away at once.
step.kpMove.done: Exactly. From h3 the knight was watching g1, and now it stands on it. The same idea as with the b-pawn, on the other side.
step.t_rook: White to move. A rook's pawn on the sixth, and the white king far away. Where does the knight need to go, and which move starts it?
step.t_rook.hint1: The knight can only reach a rook's pawn from one side. The good squares are the ones that watch h2.
step.t_rook.hint2: A check gains the tempo for the knight to reach g4.
step.rookWhy: The rook's pawn is the knight's worst enemy: it can only be approached from one side, and in the corner the knight has very few squares. But with the pawn on the sixth it can still be done. The idea is to watch h2, from g4 or f1, or to sit on h2. 1.Ne3+ gains the tempo, and 2.Ng4 is already on the right square. Notice that the target is h2, not h1: in the corner the knight has almost no way out.
step.d_rook: Watch the knight dance between g4, h2, e3 and f1, always keeping an eye on h2.
step.d_rook.m2: 1...Ke2. The black king heads towards the pawn.
step.d_rook.m3: 2.Ng4. From g4 the knight watches h2.
step.d_rook.m5: 3.Nh2, check. The knight sits in front of the pawn.
step.d_rook.m9: 5.Ne3. If 5...h2 now, 6.Nf1+ gives check and picks up the pawn.
step.d_rook.m11: 6.Nf1. From f1 the knight watches h2 and cannot be driven away in time. A draw.
step.seventh: Now the rook's pawn on the seventh, with the black king on g3. The knight on g1 stands right next to h1, but it does not watch it. The squares from which it would watch h1 are g3 and f2, and the black king occupies one and guards the other. White to move loses: the pawn queens. A rook's pawn on the seventh with its king beside it almost always beats the knight. That is why the knight has to arrive earlier, while the pawn is still on the sixth.
step.rookMove: White to move and draw. A rook's pawn on the sixth. Start with a check and keep the knight close to h2.
step.rookMove.hint: The check takes the knight to a square that watches h2. If the pawn moves, look for another check.
step.rookMove.done: That's it. Check on g4, 2.Ne3 eyeing f1, and when the pawn went to h2, 3.Nf1+ caught it.
step.t_king: Black to move, but think as White. The pawn is on the seventh and the knight on g3 looks lost. The white king is on b7, far away. How does White draw?
step.t_king.hint1: Look at which squares near the black king the knight on g3 watches. Where can the black king not go?
step.t_king.hint2: Even if the knight falls, a white king on f2 locks the black king in the corner.
step.kingWhy: This position is Dvoretsky's. The knight watches e2 and e4: if the black king goes to e3 or d2, 2.Nf1+ forks king and pawn. So the black king has to take the long way round, and every move it spends is a move for the white king. The white king's target is f2: with the black king on h1 and the pawn on h2, Black has no moves. A draw, even without the knight.
step.d_king: Watch the race of the kings. You play White.
step.d_king.m1: 1...Kd4. The black king avoids e3 and d2 because of the fork, and goes round.
step.d_king.m2: 2.Kc6. My king runs for the centre.
step.d_king.m4: 3.Kc5. I don't need to move the knight yet.
step.d_king.m6: 4.Nh1. The knight goes into the corner, in front of the pawn.
step.d_king.m8: 5.Kd4. Every black king move is a move for mine.
step.d_king.m10: 6.Ke3. My king is almost on f2.
step.d_king.m12: 7.Kf2. The black king is locked on h1, behind its own pawn. A draw.
step.kingMove: White to move and draw. The black king has already gone round to d4. Run your king towards f2, and use the knight only when you must.
step.kingMove.hint: The white king comes down the diagonal to the centre, heading for f2. The knight only moves when it is attacked, and it goes to h1.
step.kingMove.done: Perfect. The knight gained the time, the king reached f2, and the black king was locked in the corner.
step.t_stamma: White to move. King and knight against king and pawn: usually it is the knight trying to draw. Here White wins. How?
step.t_stamma.hint1: The black king is trapped in the corner, and its own pawn takes away a2 when the king is on a1.
step.t_stamma.hint2: With the black king on a1, a knight check is mate. Be careful not to stalemate.
step.stammaWhy: The white king on c2 takes away b1, b2 and b3. The black king has only a1 and a2. When the pawn goes to a2, the king on a1 has no squares left, and a knight check is mate. The pawn that should help becomes its own king's wall. This mate is named after Philipp Stamma, who published a chess book in 1737.
step.d_stamma: Watch the mate. Count the tempi: Black cannot stand still.
step.d_stamma.m1: 1.Nb4, check. The black king goes to the corner.
step.d_stamma.m3: 2.Kc1. A waiting move: the black king has no moves, so the pawn must advance.
step.d_stamma.m4: 2...a2. The pawn blocks its own king's last exit.
step.nogueiras: This happened in Nogueiras against Gongora, Cuban championship 2001. Black took White's last pawn, thinking the ending was a draw. It was not: the black king was stuck on a2, in front of its own pawn, and the white king and knight built Stamma's mate. Here White is to move: the king goes to c2, and the knight arrives at the right moment.
step.stammaMove: White to move and win, like Nogueiras. Lock the king in the corner and bring the knight in for the mate.
step.stammaMove.hint: First the king to c2. Then the knight looks for the way to c1, and from there comes the final check.
step.stammaMove.done: Mate! The pawn on a2 took its own king's last square. Gongora resigned one move earlier.
step.t_recap: White to move and draw. Before the game, one minute: which square matters, and with which move does the knight get to it?
step.t_recap.hint1: The pawn queens on c1. A check takes the knight to a square from which it watches c2 and b3.
step.recap: Three rules. First: the knight stops the pawn on the queening square, or from a square that watches it; when chased away, it comes back with check or from the other side. Second: if it cannot stand in front, it goes to the side, with the fork ready; from behind it almost never works. Third: the king helps, even from far away, and sometimes locking the enemy king in the corner is enough.
step.recapEdge: And the edge: the closer the pawn is to it, the worse for the knight. A knight's pawn demands the right square; a rook's pawn on the sixth can still be held, from g4 or f1; on the seventh, with its king beside it, it is almost always too late. And don't forget the corner: with the king trapped in front of its own rook's pawn, it is the knight that wins.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. White to move and draw: check, side control, and never lose sight of the pawn.
ex.e09: White to move and draw. The black king is in the corner and the g-pawn is running. King and knight together.
ex.e09.hint: The knight goes into the pawn's path; the white king takes squares from the black king, and the checks gain the time.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Nd6 g3, 2.Kf8, close to the black king, g2, 3.Nf7+ Kh7, 4.Ng5+ and then 5.Nf3 or 5.Nh3, watching g1. The checks gave the time that was missing. 1.Kf8 first also draws. A position by Hanneman, from perdomod's study.
ex.e10: White to move and win. The knight is far away, but the black king cannot leave the corner. Which way does the knight come?
ex.e10.hint: The knight has to reach b4 or c1, the mating squares. It comes through the centre.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Nf5! and 2.Nd4: the knight comes through the centre towards the mating squares, while the black king can only shuffle in the corner. Other moves miss the right timing for Stamma's mate.
key.front: The pawn is one step from promoting and the white king is far away. Even so, the knight on its own watches the promotion square and draws.
key.side: The knight arrives from the side, with check, on a square from which it threatens a fork if the pawn promotes. Only this route draws; checking from behind loses.
key.averbakh: Knight pawn: near the edge the knight has fewer squares, and only one route arrives in time. With it, White draws.
key.rookPawn: Rook pawn: the edge takes squares away from the knight, and nearly everything loses. Only one check brings the knight to watch the square in front of the pawn.
key.grigoriev: Rook pawn and the white king far away: the knight needs one exact check to arrive in time, and then it draws.
key.dvoretsky: The king helps: while the knight holds the pawn, the white king comes closer and shuts the black king in the corner. Draw.
key.stamma: Stamma's mate: the black king is trapped in the corner by its own pawn, and king and knight deliver mate. White wins, whoever moves.
key.nogueiras: Nogueiras against Gongora, Cuban championship, 2001: Black captured White's last pawn thinking it was a draw, and fell into Stamma's mate.
history: Knight against pawn is the ending where a knight has to stop a pawn racing to promote. Most of the time it manages, but it has an enemy: the edge of the board. Near it the knight has few squares, and a rook pawn or knight pawn can get away. It looks simple and isn't: often only one knight route draws, and everything else loses. The classic positions carry the names of the Soviet masters who studied them, such as Grigoriev, Averbakh and Dvoretsky. And there's an old surprise: with the black king trapped in the corner by its own pawn, king and knight can mate. It's Stamma's mate, named after Philipp Stamma, born in Aleppo, Syria, who published it in a book in 1737. In 2001, at the Cuban championship, a player captured his opponent's last pawn thinking it was a draw, and walked into that very mate.
practice: Now the real ending: your knight against a c-pawn on the seventh, with the black king close by. Check, side control, fork. Choose your time control and hold the draw.
ex.e11: White to move and draw. The b-pawn is two squares from queening and the knight is far away, on d7. Which way does it arrive in time?
ex.e11.hint: Look for a square from which the knight watches b2 and which the black king cannot take or box in at once.
ex.e11.solution: 2.Nb6! Kd3, 3.Na4! and the knight watches b2. After 3...Kc4, 4.Nb2+, and the knight keeps circling between a4, b2 and d3, always eyeing the square in front of the pawn. The first two moves are the only ones. It is the same right-square idea against the knight's pawn, on other squares. A position by I. Rabinovich, from perdomod's study (it starts after 1...b3).
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Two connected black pawns against the knight, and the black king is already in the corner. Which pawn does the knight let go?
ex.e12.hint: Take a pawn in such a way that, from the square where the knight lands, it watches the other pawn's queening square.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Nf4! g2, 2.Nxh3: the knight takes the h-pawn and from h3 watches g1. 2...Kh2, 3.Kf2!, and the g-pawn cannot move; if 3...Kxh3, 4.Kg1 and it falls. All three moves are the only ones: chasing the g-pawn loses. A study by M. Liburkin, Izvestia, 1932, from Bijbrengen's study.
ex.e13: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1932. The h-pawn is still at home, but the knight is in the opposite corner of the board.
ex.e13.hint: The knight must reach g4 or f1 before the pawn reaches the seventh. Count the tempi and look for the route that ends with a check.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Nb4! h5, 2.Nc6! Ke4, 3.Na5!! Kf3, 4.Nc4 h4, 5.Ne5+! Kg3, 6.Nc4, and from here 7.Ne3 and 8.Nf1 watch h2 (the ending the lesson showed with the pawn on the sixth). The route through a5 looks odd, but it is the only one that brings the knight to e5 with check at the right moment. Almost every move is the only one; only on the fourth does 4.Nc6 also work. A study by N. Grigoriev, Izvestia, 1932, from Bijbrengen's study.
ex.e14: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1938. The white king is far away and the b-pawn needs only three moves.
ex.e14.hint: A check to start. After that, sometimes the way to the front of the pawn goes backwards.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Nc7+! Kc4, 2.Ne8!! Kd3, 3.Nd6, and the knight catches the pawn: 3...Kc3 4.Ne4+ Kd3 5.Nc5+ Kd4 6.Nb3+ Kc3 7.Na5 b3 8.Nxb3. The retreat to e8 is the only move: from there the knight goes to d6, where it can jump to b5, c4 or e4. On the third move, 3.Nc7 also works. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1938, from Bijbrengen's study.
ex.e15: White to move and draw. A study by D. Gurgenidze, 1970. The knight is stuck on h7 and there are two black pawns, far apart.
ex.e15.hint: Split the work: the king takes care of one pawn; the knight, gaining time with a check, of the other.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Ka3! Kf7, 2.Kb4 Kg6, 3.Nf8+! Kf5, 4.Nd7 h5, 5.Nc5 Kg4, 6.Kxb5: the king has the b-pawn, and the knight, which left the corner with check, is already on its way to the h-pawn (7.Ne6, 8.Ng5, 9.Nh3). Up to 5.Nc5 every White move is the only one. A study by D. Gurgenidze, 64, 1970, from Bijbrengen's study.
ex.e16: White to move and draw. A study by N. Grigoriev, 1932. The knight is in the corner and the white king is far from the h-pawn.
ex.e16.hint: The knight alone cannot stop this pawn. Its job is to gain time for the white king, even by giving itself up.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Nf7! Kd4, 2.Ng5 Ke3, 3.Kd6 Kf4, 4.Nh3+! Kg3, 5.Ng1 Kg2, 6.Ne2!! Kf3, 7.Ke5! Kxe2, 8.Kf4, and the white king arrives in time: 8...Kf2 9.Kg4 h3 10.Kxh3. The knight gave itself up to pull the black king out of the way. 1.Nf7, 4.Nh3+ and 6.Ne2 are the only moves; on the last one, 7.Ng1+ also works. A study by N. Grigoriev, 64, 1932, from Bijbrengen's study.
